n0001.title: A Theory of Bugs
n0001.gist: Simple programs can compute anything complex, so unexpected bugs are often unavoidable rather than mere human error.
n0001.question: Bugs — why do they arise even in simple, carefully designed programs? (a ruliology-based theory)

n0002.title: My Program Did the Wrong Thing
n0002.gist: Bugs seem like unique accidents, but simple programs can secretly perform sophisticated computation, making unexpected and unforeseeable behavior a basic, unavoidable feature of computation itself.
n0002.question: Bugs — can a general theory explain why simple programs produce unexpected behavior? (introduces computational irreducibility)

n0007.title: “My Program Did the Wrong Thing!”
n0007.gist: Programs that run simple fragments can still perform computation as sophisticated as any system, so their behavior can exceed what our simple mental model predicts, producing bugs.

n0015.title: Bugs in Turing Machines
n0015.gist: Even tiny Turing machines meant to compute simple functions like adding one can run correctly for many inputs before suddenly failing, showing bugs emerge from genuine computational complexity, not just sloppy design.
n0015.question: Turing machines — how far must one test before a hidden bug finally appears? (several worked examples)

n0016.title: A Simple Turing Machine Bug
n0016.gist: A small Turing machine meant to add one to its input works correctly for small numbers but suddenly outputs the wrong value at input 7, revealing a genuine computational glitch.

n0029.title: How Common Are Correct Machines?
n0029.gist: Among thousands of small Turing machines that correctly add one, some behave simply while others are deceptively complex, and even these can hide bugs that first appear only at large inputs like 15.

n0043.title: Bugs in Larger Machines
n0043.gist: Among millions of four-state Turing machines that compute n+1 correctly for many steps, some still fail unexpectedly at much larger inputs, with the riskiest inputs being those whose binary form is all ones.

n0051.title: Specifying and Detecting Bugs
n0051.gist: What counts as a bug depends on the specification chosen, and across many kinds of specifications and example systems, some instances always seem to eventually escape and misbehave.
n0051.question: Specifications — can any precise requirement reliably rule out bugs in advance? (several test cases)

n0052.title: What Counts as a Bug?
n0052.gist: Whether something counts as a bug depends entirely on the specification used to judge a program, whether restating it differently, forbidding certain behaviors, or requiring certain output properties, and bugs can hide in any of these.

n0077.title: A Cellular Automaton Example
n0077.gist: Cellular automata designed to double an input's size can run correctly for a long stretch of cases before suddenly failing at some larger input, mirroring the same pattern seen with Turing machines.

n0091.title: Can One Tell If There's Going to Be a Bug?
n0091.gist: Visually simple cellular-automaton patterns are clearly bug-free, but for visually complex ones only a detailed structural argument, not mere pattern-watching, can sometimes prove that the system will always stabilize correctly.
n0091.sourceHeading: Can One Tell If There's Going to Be a Bug?

n0125.title: Formal Proofs and Irreducibility
n0125.gist: Symbolic proofs can sometimes formally establish that a program has no bugs, but building such proofs takes real computational work comparable to just running the program, and fails under genuine irreducibility.
n0125.question: Formal proofs — can proof alone guarantee a program is bug-free without running it? (worked Turing-machine proofs)

n0126.title: But What about Formal Proofs?
n0126.gist: By representing Turing-machine tapes and rules as symbolic expressions, one can sometimes construct a finite inductive proof that a machine always computes the right answer, but no such proof exists for a machine that actually has a bug.

n0174.title: Computational Irreducibility and Bugs
n0174.gist: Bugs ultimately trace back to computational irreducibility, the fact that a program's behavior often cannot be predicted without running it, though pockets of predictability can still guarantee the absence of specific kinds of bugs.

n0185.title: Testing, Induction, and Surprises
n0185.gist: Testing many cases and generalizing by induction can fail badly in computation, because rare but real bugs can lurk arbitrarily far out, hidden by pockets of apparent regularity.
n0185.question: Testing — can running enough sample cases ever prove a program has no bugs? (no, several surprise examples)

n0186.title: Did I Test Enough Cases? The Failure of Ruliological Induction
n0186.gist: Scientific induction, assuming a pattern seen many times will always hold, can fail in computation because bugs may be extremely rare yet real, hiding past whatever number of cases one happens to test.
n0186.sourceHeading: Did I Test Enough Cases? The Failure of Ruliological Induction

n0198.title: Some Typical Ruliological Surprises
n0198.gist: Across cellular automata, Turing machines, combinators, and multiway graphs, long stretches of seemingly regular or predictable behavior repeatedly give way to sudden, genuinely unexpected departures after enough steps or cases.

n0230.title: Bugs in Mathematics and Practice
n0230.gist: Mathematics mostly avoids ruliology-style bugs by focusing on human-understandable structures, while writing genuinely bug-free software means choosing well-designed primitives and visually inspecting what programs actually do inside.
n0230.question: Bugs — why does mathematics mostly escape them while software does not, and what practically helps? (a comparison and recommendations)

n0231.title: Mathematical “Bugs”
n0231.gist: Mathematical conjectures can also have distant counterexamples, like a polynomial factor coefficient that first exceeds one at a huge exponent, but mathematics mostly avoids such bugs by focusing on human-graspable, reducible structures.

n0246.title: Bugs in Practice
n0246.gist: Avoiding bugs in practice depends on choosing a well-designed language whose primitives match human intent, and on visually inspecting a program's actual internal behavior rather than merely trying to foresee or prove it.
